title: Ezekiel 7:14–27
context: The LORD’s oracle against the land continues. Though the trumpet sounds, no one goes to battle (7:14); sword is outside and famine and pestilence within (7:15). Those who escape will be on the mountains moaning like doves (7:16), with weakness, sackcloth, and shame (7:17–18). Silver and gold cannot deliver them in the day of the LORD’s wrath (7:19; compare Zephaniah 1:18). What is described as the beauty of his ornament, often read as the temple, has been defiled with idols and will be profaned by strangers (7:20–22); the identification is widely held but the notes hold it with some care. The LORD calls for chains, for the land is full of violence (7:23–24). People will seek peace, vision, law, and counsel and find none (7:25–26; compare Jeremiah 18:18), and king, prince, and people alike will mourn (7:27). Both traditions read the unit as sober judgment that ends, as the whole section does, with the people coming to know the LORD.

verses.text: They have blown the trumpet, and have made all ready; but no one goes to the battle, for my wrath is on all its multitude.
verses.arminianNotes: The trumpet sounds and preparations are made, but no one goes to battle, for wrath is on all. Arminian readers see a people paralyzed, unable to act on their own defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the failure of military readiness as showing that God has removed their strength. Both traditions read the verse as a picture of collapse, where all human preparation proves useless.

verses.text: “ ‘The sword is outside, and the pestilence and the famine within. He who is in the field will die by the sword. He who is in the city will be devoured by famine and pestilence.
verses.arminianNotes: The sword is outside and pestilence and famine within; field and city alike bring death. Arminian readers see no safe place, inside or outside the walls, for those under judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with 5:12 and 6:12, which use the same triad. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stark siege reality, described soberly and without elaboration.

verses.text: But of those who escape, they will escape and will be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, everyone in his iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who escape will be on the mountains like doves, moaning, each in his iniquity. Arminian readers see survival accompanied by grief over sin, the beginning of honest reckoning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the escape as real but sorrowful, with each person bearing his own guilt. Both traditions read the image of moaning doves as lament, and they connect it carefully to the remnant word in 6:8–9.

verses.text: All hands will be feeble, and all knees will be weak as water.
verses.arminianNotes: All hands will be feeble and all knees weak as water. Arminian readers see the physical effect of terror, as courage drains away before the coming disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing human strength failing when God’s judgment comes. Shared ground: both traditions read the image as vivid but restrained, a common biblical way of describing fear.

verses.text: They will also clothe themselves with sackcloth, and horror will cover them. Shame will be on all faces, and baldness on all their heads.
verses.arminianNotes: They will wear sackcloth, horror will cover them, and shame and baldness will mark them. Arminian readers see the customary signs of mourning taken up by a grieving people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outward signs reflecting inward shame before God. Both traditions read the verse as describing ancient mourning practices, explained briefly in context and not dwelt upon.

verses.text: They will cast their silver in the streets, and their gold will be as an unclean thing. Their silver and their gold won’t be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD’s wrath. They won’t satisfy their souls or fill their bellies; because it has been the stumbling block of their iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: They will throw silver and gold into the streets, for wealth cannot deliver them in the day of the LORD’s wrath. Arminian readers see wealth exposed as a false hope that people had trusted instead of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the close parallel with Zephaniah 1:18 by reference, and the description of wealth as a stumbling block. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as warning against trusting riches for security.

verses.text: As for the beauty of his ornament, he set it in majesty; but they made the images of their abominations and their detestable things therein. Therefore I have made it to them as an unclean thing.
verses.arminianNotes: The beauty of his ornament, set in majesty, was filled with abominable images, so it becomes unclean to them. Arminian readers often read the ornament as the temple, defiled by idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise commonly see the temple here, while some read the phrase as the people’s precious things. Both traditions read the verse as holy things corrupted by false worship, and they hold the identification with some care.

verses.text: I will give it into the hands of the strangers for a prey, and to the wicked of the earth for a plunder; and they will profane it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will give it to strangers and the wicked of the earth as plunder, and they will profane it. Arminian readers see the people’s defilement of holy things answered by outsiders profaning them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God handing over what he had given, as a just consequence of its misuse. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as measure-for-measure judgment, with foreign invaders as the instruments.

verses.text: I will also turn my face from them, and they will profane my secret place. Robbers will enter into it, and profane it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will turn his face away, and robbers will profane his secret place. Arminian readers see the withdrawal of God’s protective presence, leaving the sanctuary open to violation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the secret place as likely the inner sanctuary, now given up by the LORD himself. Both traditions read the turning of God’s face as the deepest loss, and they anticipate the departure of the glory in chapters 10–11.

verses.text: “ ‘Make chains, for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says to make chains, for the land is full of bloody crimes and violence. Arminian readers see chains as a sign of coming captivity, matching the injustice that filled the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse naming social violence, alongside idolatry, as a cause of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining the worship of God with justice toward neighbors.

verses.text: Therefore I will bring the worst of the nations, and they will possess their houses. I will also make the pride of the strong to cease. Their holy places will be profaned.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will bring the worst of the nations to possess their houses and profane their holy places. Arminian readers see the humbling of the proud as invaders take what the people thought secure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using even harsh nations to accomplish his purposes, without approving their wickedness. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as the end of the pride of the strong and the loss of what was held holy.

verses.text: Destruction comes! They will seek peace, and there will be none.
verses.arminianNotes: Destruction comes; they will seek peace, and there will be none. Arminian readers see the bitter result of having ignored earlier calls to turn, when peace was still offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast with false prophets who promised peace, compare Jeremiah 6:14 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the failure of every hope that is not grounded in the LORD.

verses.text: Mischief will come on mischief, and rumor will be on rumor. They will seek a vision of the prophet; but the law will perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders.
verses.arminianNotes: Disaster follows disaster; they seek a vision, but law perishes from priest and counsel from elders. Arminian readers see guidance withdrawn when the people finally seek it, too late.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal of Jeremiah 18:18 by reference, where opponents claimed law would not perish from the priest. Both traditions read the verse as a famine of guidance, and they name the parallel without harmonizing.

verses.text: The king will mourn, and the prince will be clothed with desolation. The hands of the people of the land will be troubled. I will do to them after their way, and according to their own judgments I will judge them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: King, prince, and people will mourn; the LORD will judge them according to their ways, and they will know that he is the LORD. Arminian readers see judgment reaching every level of society, fitting their deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the closing refrain gathering Ezekiel 4–7 to its goal: the knowledge of the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober ending, in which judgment serves to make the LORD known.
